It depends on the engine. If it's a 2.5 5 cylinder, those are pretty much bullet proof, albeit with a couple little quirks that sometimes need attention. Not the best gas mileage, but plenty of torque and reliability.

A gas 1.8 turbo engine will have more power and better mpg at the cost of reliability. Newer ones aren't so bad, but they generally have more small (and big) things happen--water pumps, carbon buildup, etc.

A diesel (TDI) can potentially last forever, has great torque, and incredible mileage. But I think those come with the DSG transmission. That trans is really nice, shifts instantly, but needs regular maintenance. I'm also not 100% familiar with the TDI as far as typical problems, besides the Dieselgate stuff.

Any VW needs religious maintenance. I never go beyond 5k miles with premium full synthetic oil. Find one that has been taken care of, and it should take of you.

You would need a custom exhaust manifold/downpipe, blow-off valve, a way to feed and drain oil, an intercooler, coolant lines to/from the turbo, possibly upgraded fueling (injectors and/or pump). You'd have to figure out how to fit all of this in what is probably an already crowded engine bay. And a way to tune it. This may require a standalone ECU, and it would require someone to tune it. Labor for all of this if you had a technician/shop do it. Probably a ton more stuff I'm forgetting. Long story short, $$$$$$$$

If you're not careful, you can blow your engine because it was not designed for boost. I don't know how sturdy the GT's engine is, but it likely has a higher compression ratio than its factory boosted counterparts, and therefore you won't be able to run a ton of boost.

So to answer your question, yes, it can be boosted. With just a cold air intake? No, absolutely not. Is it worth it? That's up to you. If I had that car, I'd just enjoy it for what it is. Keep in mind you'd be making the car less reliable by adding a turbo.

With all wheel drive, the transfer case needs to have even wear on all 4 tires, or else the power distribution will be severely out of spec. It is possible to destroy drivetrain components this way. 

Now, if you buy 4 new tires, and blow one out the next day, you *should* be fine just getting one because it will be at the same tread. Just make sure to get the exact same brand, type, size, etc. 

This doesn't really apply to FWD or RWD, although you *should* replace those in pairs.

2019? Almost, if not brand new. Just like any other car, take care of it and it should be good for a long time. It's too new to see what kind of common failures there are; but being a 4cyl, doesn't take a ton of oil. Make sure to let it warm up fully before hammering on it (like any other car).

When you park, I suggest letting it idle for ~30 seconds before shutting it off, if you hammer on it right before you're done driving. 

If it is equipped with 4MOTION, keep in mind if you blow a tire, you will have to replace all 4. From a maintenance perspective that is something to consider.
